The dispute is where Patrick Flynn was born — Ireland or Pennsylvania. This matters because it bears on when the Flynn family immigrated, which in turn affects the search for Patrick's parents in Irish records versus Pennsylvania records.

The Ireland claim comes from two separate U.S. census records: the 1850 census of Schuylkill County and the 1860 census of the same county, both showing Patrick in the Thomas Flynn household. In each case, an enumerator visited the home and recorded birthplace from whoever answered the door — most likely a Flynn family member who knew the family's Irish origins firsthand. fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County census records both state Ireland, while his 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. This matters directly to q_001 — identifying Patrick's parents — because birthplace shapes where pre-immigration records might be sought.

The 1850 census (src_001) lists Patrick, age 5, as born in Ireland, reported by an unidentified household member who was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife. The 1860 census (src_003) again shows Patrick, age 15, in the same Thomas Flynn household in the same county, with Ireland again given as his birthplace and the same household-informant logic applying. The 1908 death certificate (src_004) states Pennsylvania as the birthplace; the named informant is James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law.

Ireland is the more reliable answer. Thomas Flynn and his wife, present in the household when Patrick was a child, had firsthand knowledge of where their son was born. Two separate government enumerations, ten years apart and taken by different enumerators, recorded that same answer consistently. James Brown, by contrast, married into the family and was reporting a fact about an event that occurred roughly 60 years before he provided the information — he could only have known what he was told, if he was told at all.

The Pennsylvania answer on the death certificate is best explained by the immigration-origin confusion pattern: a son-in-law reporting a birth he did not witness, decades later, from fragmentary family knowledge, in a state where the family had lived for his entire adult experience of them. Pennsylvania was the locally familiar answer — it was where Patrick lived, where his children grew up, and where James Brown knew him. Asked for a birthplace by a registrar in 1908, a son-in-law could reasonably have substituted the family's American home for the Irish origin he may never have been told about, or had forgotten. This is a well-documented pattern in death certificates for immigrants: informants conflate where the person lived with where they were born. Assertion a_002 (Ireland, 1850 census) is preferred, corroborated by a_009 (Ireland, 1860 census).
